strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving that nested submodel learning recovers the Pareto front while post-training selection and all-submodel learning fail (Theorems 4.1-4.3 for linear models)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse architectures (LLaMA 1B/3B/8B, ViT-L/H/7B, GPT-2) showing consistent improvements in graceful degradation
Figure 3 demonstrates FLEXRANK recovers true Pareto front on toy models, validating core theoretical insight
Well-motivated practical problem with clear 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' paradigm
Detailed implementation for multiple layer types (linear, convolutional, attention) with explicit hyperparameters
weaknesses: Severe training limitation: only 10,000 steps (~0.5 epoch) due to computational constraints, with authors acknowledging 'expected improvements with additional compute' but providing no concrete evidence of convergence or final performance

Theory-practice gap: Theorems 4.1-4.3 are proven only for linear models, but the method is applied to complex non-linear networks with activations and skip connections; the generalization is not rigorously justified

Critical assumptions inadequately validated: (1) additivity assumption for layer errors (Section 3.2) acknowledged as 'strong' but no empirical validation of violation magnitude; (2) relative importance ordering preservation through training is assumed but not proven for non-linear case

Unfair experimental comparisons: FLEXRANK uses knowledge distillation for refinement while SVD/DataSVD baselines and ACIP do not; missing ablation comparing FLEXRANK without distillation to SVD with distillation

Limited novelty: data-aware SVD (Chen et al. 2021), dynamic programming for allocation, and knowledge distillation are all established; main contribution is the nested structure constraint, which is incremental
Incomplete practical deployment evaluation: no wall-clock inference speeds, actual hardware deployment results, or guidance on runtime submodel selection
Dynamic programming validity unclear: DP is exact only under additivity assumption (which is violated); no comparison of DP-selected configurations to oracle optimal ones
Missing comparisons with FlexTron (Cai et al., 2024) and LlamaFlex (Cai et al., 2025), the most recent elastic model training methods, despite addressing the same problem
No sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (α_k weights in Eq. 6, calibration dataset size/distribution, DP layer-wise error estimates)
Limited statistical rigor: no significance tests on performance differences; Table 1 shows improvements are sometimes small relative to variance; Figures 4-5 lack error bars

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving why nested submodel training recovers Pareto fronts (Theorems 4.1-4.3), with clear insights on representational interference in competing objectives
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse architectures (CNNs, ViTs, LLMs) and tasks (NLP, CV) with extensive ablations and controlled experiments validating core claims
Practical system design with DataSVD initialization, efficient O(L·K) DP algorithm, and GAR reparametrization that translates theoretical savings to measured speedups (Figure 10)
Consistently strong empirical results showing graceful performance degradation (70% compression with <5% drop on ViTs) and competitive with or outperforming multiple baselines
Honest treatment of limitations, detailed reproducibility information with promised code release, and thorough appendices with implementation details and hyperparameters
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical results (Section 4) proved only for linear models; core DP assumption (additive errors across layers) validated empirically only on MNIST (4-layer network), not on actual LLMs or large ViTs where nonlinearity may violate assumptions

Ranking-preservation assumption (page 3) asserted rather than proven for deep nonlinear networks; no analysis of when this assumption breaks down or sensitivity to violations; insufficient justification for why this holds in complex networks with nonlinear dependencies

Limited technical novelty: DataSVD acknowledged as not new, distillation and low-rank decomposition are standard, GAR explicitly stated as not exclusive to FlexRank; primary novelty is combination rather than fundamental innovation

Incomplete experimental design: sensitivity to calibration data size/diversity not studied, LoRA finetuning shows severe degradation at 0.4× compression on code tasks (Table 1), vision experiments only on ImageNet1K, no validation of DP assumptions on large realistic networks

Non-trivial training overhead (2× memory, 2× slowdown, requires teacher-student) and inference speedups dependent on specific hardware/kernel implementations; practical adoption concerns for large-scale deployment

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem of adaptive model deployment across heterogeneous hardware
Rigorous theoretical analysis for linear models (Section 4) clearly explaining advantages of nested training over PTS/ASL
Comprehensive experiments across multiple architectures (DNNs, ViTs, LLMs) and scales with post-adaptation evaluation
Empirical validation of key assumptions with strong metrics (Spearman ρ=0.991 for ranking preservation)
Honest discussion of limitations including training efficiency costs (2× overhead) and theory-practice gap
Clear presentation of three-stage methodology with well-motivated pipeline
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DataSVD (not new per authors), DP rank selection, and distillation are standard techniques; contribution is primarily their combination
Critical theory-practice gap: Theoretical guarantees only for linear models; no justification for why linear theory predicts behavior on deep nonlinear networks with complex interactions
Ranking-preservation assumption validated only on toy 10×10 linear problem on MNIST, not on actual LLM/ViT layers where method is applied
Unfair experimental comparisons: LAYERSKIP trained on 839B tokens vs FLEXRANK's 5B (167× difference), confounding training cost with method quality
Missing key ablation: No isolated analysis of distillation vs. nested structure contribution; Figure 7(b) suggests distillation is doing most of the work
DP assumes additive errors across layers, known to be violated in deep networks; paper acknowledges this simplification but proceeds without analyzing failure modes
Modest improvements over simpler baselines: Independent submodel training comparison (Figure 5) shows small gaps with no statistical significance testing; no error bars on any results
Algorithm clarity: SELECTPROFILES function (Algorithm 1, line 13) undefined; how 'best budget profiles' are selected is unclear
Design choice unjustified: Ranks fixed from initialization rather than jointly optimized; why constrain solution unnecessarily?
Inference efficiency underspecified: Figure 10 only for specific matrix sizes; no end-to-end latency measurements or actual deployment costs

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation with rigorous proofs (Theorems 4.1-4.3) characterizing why nested submodel learning is necessary for Pareto optimality in the linear case
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse architectures (CNNs, ViTs, LLMs) with both zero-shot and downstream task evaluation
Novel insight that nestedness is critical for avoiding weight-sharing interference, with clear formalization of Pareto elastic models (Definition 2.1)
Practical 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' framework with consistent improvements over rank-based baselines (ACIP, DataSVD, SVD)
Well-designed ablations isolating key components (Fig. 6-8): importance of nested training, calibration data size, layer initialization
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes in Section 7
GAR reparametrization provides theoretical and practical inference speedups (Fig. 10)
Clear presentation with rigorous proofs in appendices and detailed algorithmic descriptions
weaknesses: Central assumption of ranking preservation (additive error probe across layers) is validated only on toy MNIST problem with 4 layers; no validation on realistic 70+ layer Transformers where assumption likely violates more severely
Gap between theory (rigorous linear case proofs) and practice (deep nonlinear networks) not formally bridged; Theorems 4.1-4.3 do not apply to actual networks

Modest empirical improvements over strong baselines: Fig. 5 shows FLEXRANK only 'slightly outperforms' independently trained submodels at matched budget, suggesting weight-sharing benefits are limited

Training efficiency concerns: 2× memory overhead and ~2× slowdown preventing fused kernels; calibration uses only 5B tokens vs. 9T in original training (1800× reduction) with unclear impact on quality
Calibration dataset sensitivity not thoroughly analyzed; requires representative data Z but minimal investigation of distribution mismatch effects
DP algorithm quality depends on violated assumptions; no formal characterization of solution degradation when additive error assumption breaks down in realistic networks
End-to-end inference latency measurements missing; practical speedups validated only on specific matrix sizes (Fig. 10), not on realistic models across diverse hardware

Limited scope: specialized to low-rank compression without exploring combinations with pruning, quantization, or depth-based elasticity; minimal comparison with architectural elasticity methods (Flextron, LlamaFlex only in appendix)
